title: Creating a Competition for Innovation
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that innovation can't be mandated or fully structured, but it can be encouraged by turning it into a competition. It highlights research showing that a single grand prize engages far fewer people than several smaller rewards spread across the organization. It also recommends that peers, not senior leaders, judge submitted ideas, since junior staff both understand feasibility better and reduce the fear of harsh judgment from the top. The conclusion frames competitive structures as a reliable way to seed a broader innovation mindset.
points: Innovation can't be mandated by leaders, but contest structures can encourage it organically.
Several smaller prizes drive more participation than one grand prize.
Peer judges, rather than senior leaders, are recommended for evaluating submitted ideas.
Using peer judges reduces team members' fear of being harshly judged for a wild idea.
Repeated contests can seed a lasting innovation mindset across the whole organization.
quotes: Getting team members to innovate and think creatively is not something leaders can mandate.
As it turns out, the best way to promote innovation is to ask team members to compete for it.
While a grand prize fosters excitement, offering several smaller but valuable rewards encourages more participation across the enterprise.
Best practice is not to have the most senior leaders judge the utility and value of the ideas. Instead, turn to peers to make the evaluations.
They recognize that the real contest is to make the organization better.
